lessons.title: Managing the flock environment and nutrition
lessons.html:
Managing the flock environment and nutrition

At management level, husbandry means designing and controlling the systems that let birds express their genetic potential: environment, nutrition, water and welfare. The breed company's management guide is the baseline; the manager adapts it to local conditions and monitors results.

Environment

  • Temperature: set by bird age and adjusted by observing behaviour. Chicks need high temperatures at placement, reducing as they feather. Older birds need cooling in hot weather.
  • Ventilation: minimum ventilation removes moisture, ammonia and carbon dioxide even in cold weather; tunnel or cross ventilation and evaporative cooling remove heat in summer.
  • Relative humidity: too high causes wet litter; too low causes dust.
  • Light: intensity, duration and pattern affect growth, activity, leg health and laying. Programmes must provide a dark period for rest as the guide and welfare codes require.
  • Litter: dry, friable litter protects feet and reduces ammonia and coccidiosis.
  • Stocking density: within company, welfare code and buyer limits.

Nutrition

Feed is formulated by nutritionists for each phase - starter, grower, finisher for broilers; rearing, pre-lay and layer phases for layers. Energy, protein (amino acids such as lysine and methionine), calcium and phosphorus, vitamins and trace minerals must be balanced. The manager ensures:

  • Correct feed phase at the correct age or weight.
  • Feed quality on delivery: no mould, correct form (crumbs or pellets), not contaminated.
  • Enough feeder space and correct feeder height.
  • Feed intake monitored daily against standard.

Water

Water quality (bacteria, minerals, pH) is tested regularly; lines are cleaned between flocks and sanitised during the flock. Drinker height and pressure are adjusted as birds grow. Daily water meter readings and the water-to-feed ratio are key indicators.

lessons.title: Flock health programmes and biosecurity
lessons.html:
Flock health programmes and biosecurity

The veterinary health plan

A poultry veterinarian designs the health plan with the manager. It includes the vaccination programme, biosecurity standards, monitoring and sampling, approved treatments, and procedures for disease outbreaks. Review it regularly against disease trends and flock results.

Vaccination management

Vaccines may be given at the hatchery or on farm by drinking water, coarse spray, eye drop, wing web or injection. Successful vaccination depends on:

  • Cold chain from supplier to bird.
  • Correct preparation, dilution and stabilisers for water vaccines.
  • Every bird receiving the dose - check water consumption timing or use dye markers.
  • Trained, supervised staff.
  • Records: date, product, batch, method, house and staff.
  • Post-vaccination serology where the vet uses it to check response.

Biosecurity programme

ElementExamples
IsolationFencing, distance between sites, wild bird exclusion
Traffic controlEntry protocols, vehicle disinfection, visitor logs, clean-to-dirty flows
SanitationShower-in, dedicated clothing, foot baths, between-flock cleaning
Pest controlRodent baiting maps, fly and beetle control
MonitoringAudits, swabs after cleaning, compliance checks

Disease monitoring

Monitor daily mortality, feed and water intake, weights, egg production and bird behaviour. Use post-mortem examinations by the vet or laboratory for abnormal mortality. Surveillance sampling for avian influenza, Newcastle disease, Salmonella and Mycoplasma may be required by the vet, buyers or compartment schemes.

Controlled diseases

Suspected avian influenza or Newcastle disease must be reported to the state veterinarian under the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984. Prepare an outbreak response plan: who to call, movement standstill, isolation, record keeping, and cooperation with official culling and disposal. Staff need support during culling, which is distressing.

lessons.title: Treatment, welfare and performance monitoring
lessons.html:
Treatment, welfare and performance monitoring

Responsible medicine use

Treatments should be based on a diagnosis by the vet. Use registered products under Act 36 of 1947 or veterinary prescriptions, at the correct dose and duration, usually through drinking water or feed. Record every treatment and enforce withdrawal periods for meat and eggs - birds or eggs must not be sold within the withdrawal period. Prudent antimicrobial use is essential to slow antimicrobial resistance, which threatens both animal and human health.

Welfare

Welfare is a legal duty under the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 and a requirement of buyers and industry codes. Indicators to monitor:

  • Mortality and culls; reasons for culling.
  • Lameness and gait scores.
  • Footpad lesions and hock burns (litter quality).
  • Feather condition and pecking injuries.
  • Panting or huddling (thermal comfort).
  • Catching and transport injuries, bruising and dead on arrival at the abattoir.

Sick or injured birds that will not recover must be culled promptly and humanely by trained staff using an approved method.

Catching and transport

Plan catching at cooler times, with trained crews who handle birds gently and do not overfill crates. Feed withdrawal before slaughter is timed to the processor's instructions. Vehicles must protect birds from heat, cold and rain.

Performance monitoring

BroilersLayers
Daily mortality, cumulative mortalityHen-day production %
Weekly weights vs standard, uniformityEgg weight, shell quality, grade-outs
FCR, efficiency indexFeed per dozen eggs
Condemnations at the abattoirBody weight and uniformity in rearing

Plot results against the breed standard and previous flocks. Investigate deviations early with the vet and nutritionist, and close each flock with a review.

Key points

  • Control temperature, ventilation, light, litter and density using the management guide.
  • Match feed phases to age and monitor feed and water intake daily.
  • Vaccinate with cold chain, correct preparation and full coverage.
  • Report controlled diseases and have an outbreak plan.
  • Use medicines prudently with withdrawal periods; monitor welfare indicators.
